'''''Agastache foeniculum''''' ([[syn.]] '''''Agastache anethiodora''''' ([[Nutt.]]) [[Nathaniel Lord Britton|Britton]]), commonly called '''anise hyssop''',<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Anise Hyssop – Roots of Medicine |url=https://dsps.lib.uiowa.edu/roots/anise-hyssop/ |access-date=2026-01-20 |website=[[University of Iowa]]}}</ref> '''blue giant hyssop''', '''Fragrant giant hyssop''', or the '''lavender giant hyssop''',{{Additional citation needed|date=January 2026}} is a species of [[perennial]] plant in the [[mint family]]. The plant is native to much of northern North America. It is tolerant of [[deer]] and drought, and is visited by many pollinators.

==Description==
Growing from a [[taproot]], the [[perennial]] plant grows to {{Convert|0.6-1.2|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} in height,<ref name="illinoi" /><ref name="botan"/> in a clumplike, upright shape. The leaves have an oval, toothed shape with a white tint underneath.<ref name="illinoi" />

The plant blooms in June to September with bright lavender [[flower]]s that become more colorful near the tip.<ref name="botan">{{cite web |title=Agastache foeniculum |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=d554 |access-date=20 December 2013 |work=Missouri Botanical Gardens}}</ref><ref name="finegar">{{cite web|title=Agastache foeniculum (Anise hyssop)|url=http://www.finegardening.com/plantguide/agastache-foeniculum-hyssop.aspx|work=Fine Gardening|access-date=20 December 2013}}</ref> One plant may produce upwards of 90,000 individual flowers.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pan |first1=Ziliang |title=Bee Visitation and Nectar Production of Anise Hyssop |url=https://ag.umass.edu/sites/ag.umass.edu/files/research-reports/1997-03-bee-visitation-and-nectar-production-of-anise-hyssop.pdf |access-date=16 August 2019}}</ref> They appear in showy [[verticillaster]]s or false whorls, occasionally branching at the apex.<ref name="illinoi">{{Illinois Wildflowers |prairie|plantx|anise_hyssopx|Anise hyssop |access-date=20 December 2013}}</ref>

{{gallery|Agastache foeniculum - Anise Hyssop (7-15-24) 03.jpg|Leaves|mode=packed}}

=== Similar species ===
''A. foeniculum'' is commonly confused with ''[[Agastache rugosa|A. rugosa]]''<ref>Roger Guillermo Fuentes-Granados. [https://dr.lib.iastate.edu/bitstreams/93628f9b-d2c7-4523-a294-c7f36dffb96e/download "Genetic Studies of Agastache."] Iowa State University PhD dissertation. 1997. p. 14. {{doi|10.31274/rtd-180813-13259}}</ref> (which is sometimes sold as ''A. foeniculum'') as well as ''[[Agastache scrophulariifolia|A. scrophulariifolia]]''.<ref>Arthur O. Tucker and Thomas DeBaggio, ''The Encyclopedia of Herbs: A Comprehensive Reference to Herbs of Flavor and Fragrance.'' Timber Press, 2009. [https://books.google.com/books?id=7_KPgxEglHAC&pg=PA127 p. 127.] {{ISBN|9781604691344}}</ref> Anise hyssop is in the same family as [[hyssop]] (the mint family Lamiaceae), but they are not closely related. Hyssop (''[[Hyssopus (plant)|Hyssopus]]'') is a genus of about 10–12 species of herbaceous or semi-woody plants native from the east [[Mediterranean]] to central Asia.<ref name="USDA">{{PLANTS|symbol=AGFO|taxon=Agastache foeniculum}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The plant is native to much of north-central and northern North America, notably the [[Great Plains]] and other [[prairie]]s.<ref name="USDA" /><ref>{{BONAP|genus=Agastache|species=foeniculum|date=2014}}</ref> 

==Ecology==
The species is tolerant of [[deer]] and drought, and attracts various potential pollinators, including [[hummingbird]]s, [[butterflies]],<ref name="botan" /> [[bumblebee]]s, [[honey bee]]s, [[carpenter bee]]s, and night-flying [[moth]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ayers |first1=George |date=July 1994 |title=The Genus Agastache as Bee Forage: An Analysis of Reader Returns |journal=American Bee Journal |issue=134 |pages=480–482}}</ref> Honey bees make a light fragrant honey from the flower's nectar.<ref name="Herbs Smithsonian Handbooks">"Herbs"; Smithsonian Handbook - Lesley Bremness</ref> The plant is considered one of the premier species for feeding pollinators. The 1969 edition of the Rodale's ''Encyclopedia of Organic Gardening'' claims that one acre of the species can support 100 honey-bee [[Beehive|hives]], the flowers blooming for a very long season, often from June until frost and during the time it blooms, one can see bees on the flowers from the morning until dusk.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rodale |first1=J.I. |title=The Encyclopedia of Organic Gardening |date=1969 |location=Emmaus Pennasylvania |pages=522–523}}</ref> The many flowers of the plant provide forage for bees, butterflies and hummingbirds.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kagan |first1=Carol |title=Anise Hyssop for the Perennial Garden |url=https://extension.psu.edu/anise-hyssop-for-the-perennial-garden |website=PennState Extension |access-date=13 August 2019}}</ref>

==Uses==
The plant was used medicinally by the [[Cree]], [[Cheyenne]], and [[Ojibwe|Ojibwa]] peoples to treat fevers, respiratory issues, and burns.<ref name=":0" /> The soft, [[anise]]-scented leaves<ref name= finegar /> are used as a seasoning, as a [[tea]], in [[potpourri]], and can be crumbled in [[salad]].
